questions.question: Which part of a flower develops into a seed?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ovule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **ovule** is the part of the flower that develops into a seed after fertilization.
 
• It is located within the ovary of the pistil, which is the female reproductive part of the flower.
 
• After fertilization, the ovule matures into a seed, while the ovary develops into a fruit.
 
• The seed contains the plant embryo along with stored food, which is essential for germination and growth.
 
• Each ovule consists of protective layers (integuments) and a central tissue called the nucellus, where the embryo sac is formed.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Parts of a Flower:**

 
 
• The flower is composed of four main parts: sepals, petals, stamens (male reproductive organs), and pistils (female reproductive organs).
 
• The pistil consists of three main parts: stigma, style, and ovary, where the ovules are housed.
 
 
 
• **Pollination and Fertilization:**
 
 
• Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther (male part) to the stigma (female part).
 
• Fertilization occurs when the male gamete in the pollen fuses with the female gamete in the ovule, forming a zygote.
 
 
 
• **Seed Development:**
 
 
• After fertilization, the zygote develops into an embryo, and the ovule transforms into a seed.
 
• The seed coat develops from the integuments of the ovule, providing protection to the embryo.
 
 
 
• **Fruit Formation:**
 
 
• While the ovule becomes the seed, the ovary of the flower develops into a fruit that protects the seeds and aids in their dispersal.

questions.question: Which of the following process helps in absorption of water and minerals from Roots to Leaves?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __Transpiration__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/9f1c944588dff7ed66b6b6cfcf334bf304849adc53aad282e7ed498dc102e74e.png] 

 
• Transpiration is a process in which loss of water vapor takes place from plants leave through the help of stomata. 
 
• It is a physical process that is under the control of both external physical and physiological factors. 
 
• Transpiration requires solar radiation for energy which is absorbed by plants. 
 
• The rate of transpiration is proportional to the gradient in water vapor concentration between sources of water within the plant and the bulk atmosphere and the total resistance to water vapor diffusion of the plant.
 
• Plant loss water from leaves and stomata largely control leaf transpiration
 
• 
 
Regulation of stomatal aperture is very complex, as stomata respond to a variety of environmental (e.g., light, humidity, temperature, CO2 concentration) and endogenous (e.g., root and leaf hormone production and release, age) influences.

 

​ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ff1ed6fc970094d35c9abdf52ce2c2c30d160c647b2f2f2427adeae9d1c6ce95.png] 

 

 
• Sedimentation is the process of deposition of a solid particle from a state of suspension or solution in a fluid with the help of gravity. The particles that settle out from the solution become sediment, and in water treatment is known as sludge.
 
• Condensation is the change of water from its gaseous form (water vapor) into liquid water. It takes place in two ways: Either the air is cooled to its dew point or it becomes so saturated with water vapor that it cannot hold any more water.
 
• Accumulation is the process of water collecting in rivers, lakes, streams, oceans and other bodies of water. When water condenses and precipitates, it eventually runs off of surfaces and collects again in bodies of water. From there, the water evaporates, and the cycle begins again. Accumulation is important for a number of reasons, both in ecosystems and for humans.

questions.question: The directional growth movement in plants due to touch is called________
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Thigmonasty.**__

 
• The plants cannot move from one place to another because the roots are fixed at the ground.
 
 
• Plants can move their** individual parts** without moving the entire body.
 
• The two types of plant movements are **tropic movement** and **nastic movement**.
 
• **Thigmonasty** is the nastic response of a plant due to touch or vibration.
 
• The directional growth movement in plants due to touch is called thigmonasty.
 
• Thigmonasty is also known as Seismonasty.
 
• **Mimosa pudica** is the best example of a thigmonasty exhibiting plant.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/83b694b757e81013d523ce9b546804c766ae4dd47ac6083e64b8eee1afc9f876.png] 
 
 
 
• **Geotropism** is the growth of the parts of plants in response to the **force of gravity**.
 
 
• The roots of a plant growing down into the ground is an example of geotropism.
 
• The upward growth of plant parts, against gravity, is called **negative geotropism**.
 
• The downward growth of roots is called **positive geotropism**.
 
 
 
• **Phototropism** is the growth of a plant in response to a** light stimulus**.
 
 
• If the plant grows towards the light source, it is called positive phototropism.
 
• If the plant grows away from the light source, it is called negative phototropism.
 
 
 
• **Chemotropism** is the growth of a plant navigated by** chemical stimulus** from outside.
 
 
• If the growth response is towards the stimulus it is called positive chemotropism.
 
• If the growth response is away from the stimulus it is called negative chemotropism.

questions.question: Which protein is found in grains?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gluten**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Gluten** is the main protein found in grains such as wheat, barley, and rye.
 
• It is a composite of storage proteins, namely gliadin and glutenin, which are conjoined with starch in the endosperm of various grass-related grains.
 
• Gluten gives dough its elasticity, helping it rise and keep its shape, and often gives the final product a chewy texture.
 
• While it is a common ingredient in many foods, some individuals have gluten intolerance or celiac disease, which requires them to follow a gluten-free diet.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Celiac disease** is an autoimmune disorder where ingestion of gluten leads to damage in the small intestine.
 
• A **gluten-free diet** involves excluding foods that contain gluten, which is found in wheat, barley, rye, and derivatives of these grains.
 
• Gluten-free products are widely available and are essential for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.
 
• Despite its necessity for some, a gluten-free diet is also adopted by others for various health benefits or lifestyle choices.

questions.question: A type of asexual reproduction in which new plants are produced from roots, stems, leaves and buds are known as:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**vegetative propagation.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **Asexual plant **propagation methods produce new plants from vegetative parts of the original plant, such as the leaves, stems and roots.
 
• These methods are generally referred to as **vegetative propagation.**
 
• The main advantage of vegetative propagation methods is that the new plants contain the genetic material of only one parent.
 
• So they are essentially clones of the parent plant. 
 
• This can also help to maintain consistent quality and taste in products made from plants or crops. 
 
• With **vegetative propagation**, plants also bypass the immature seedling phase and therefore reach the mature phase sooner.
 
• This can save a lot of time and money for commercial plant production.
 
• A plant can reproduce asexually in two ways: naturally and artificially.
 
• **Natural vegetative **propagation occurs when an axillary bud grows into a lateral shoot and develops its own roots (also known as **adventitious roots**).
 
• Plant structures allowing natural vegetative propagation include bulbs, rhizomes, stolons and tubers.
 
• **Artificial vegetative propagation: **
 
 
• Horticulturalists and gardeners also use vegetative propagation methods that plants don’t use naturally.
 
 
 
• These methods involve taking a piece of one parent plant and causing it to regenerate itself into a new plant.
 
• **Common methods include cuttings, grafting and budding, and tissue culture.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Layering propagation**:

 
 
• Layering is a method of asexual propagation in which a stem is made to produce roots while still attached to the parent plant. The parent plant provides the new plant with water and nutrients while the roots are forming. Layering can be used for plants that are difficult to propagate using other methods.
 
 
 
• **Budding propagation:**
 
 
• ​Propagation by budding is a pretty common method of plant propagation, in which a plant bud is grafted onto the stem of a rootstock plant.
 
• Trees propagated through budding include dogwood, birch, maple, mountain ash, redbud and Ginko.
 
 
 
• **Grafting propagation:**
 
 
• Grafting is a method of asexual plant propagation that joins plant parts from different plants together so they will heal and grow as one plant.
 
• This technique is used to propagate plants that do not root well from cuttings, utilize superior root systems, or maintain clonal production.

questions.question: Which of the following does **NOT **figure among the main functions of the root system of a plant?

options.text: Absorption of water from the soil
Absorption of mineral from the soil
Providing a proper anchorage to the plant parts
Supply of food to plant parts

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Supply of food to plant parts**__.

__
 
• **The supply of food to plant parts is not the main function of the root system of a plant**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **Key Points__**

 
• Plants have specialized organs that help them survive and reproduce in a great diversity of habitats. The major organs of most plants include roots, stems, and leaves.
 
• Roots are important organs in all vascular plants.
 
 
• Most vascular plants have two types of roots: primary roots that grow downward and secondary roots that branch out to the side.
 
• Together, all the roots of a plant make up a root system.
 
 
 
• A root is a complex organ consisting of several types of tissue. The structure of roots helps them perform their primary functions, which are-
 
 
• **Absorbing water and minerals**
 
 
• Thin-walled epidermal cells and root hairs are well suited to absorb water and dissolved minerals from the soil. The roots of many plants also have a mycorrhizal relationship with fungi for greater absorption.
 
 
 
• **Anchoring and supporting the plant**
 
 
• Root systems help anchor plants to the ground, allowing plants to grow tall without toppling over. A tough covering may replace the epidermis in older roots, making them ropelike and even stronger.
 
 
 
• **Storing food**
 
 
• In many plants, ground tissues in roots store food produced by the leaves during photosynthesis. The bloodroot stores food in its roots over the winter.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a pair of micronutrients?
questions.solution:
Correct Answer **Calcium and fats**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**__Concept:__

__
 
• Nutrients are the substances that are required by the organism/ plant to survive, grow, and reproduce.
 
• In the case of plants, different nutrients are absorbed by the roots and are then transported to the rest of the plant body.
 
• Xylem helps in the transportation of water, minerals, and nutrients in plants.

Explanation:__

An element is regarded as essential for a plant based on the following criteria:

 
• An element should be essential for the normal growth and reproduction of the plant.
 
• A requirement of an element should be such that it cannot be replaced by any other element.
 
• The element should be directly involved in the metabolism of the plant.

Based on the above-mentioned criteria and the quantitative requirements, nutrients are classified into two groups: Macronutrients and Micronutrients

Macronutrients:

 
• Macronutrients are needed in larger amounts by the plant tissues for their survival, growth, and other essential functions.
 
• Carbon (C), hydrogen (H), oxygen (O), nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), sulfur (S), potassium (K), calcium (Ca), and magnesium (Mg) are the macronutrients required by plants.

Micronutrients:

 
• Micronutrients are needed in smaller amounts by the plant tissues.
 
• Micronutrients required by plants are iron (Fe), manganese (Mn), copper (Cu), molybdenum (Mo), zinc (Zn), boron (B), chlorine (Cl), and nickel (Ni).
 
• Apart from these essential elements mentioned above, elements such as sodium (Na), silicon (Si), cobalt (Co), and selenium (Se) are also required by some higher plants.

questions.question: Which tissue is responsible for the flexibility in plants?
questions.solution:
The Correct Answer is __Collenchyma.__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Flexibility in plants **is due to Collenchyma.
 
• Collenchyma is the tissue present in the leaf stalks below the epidermis.
 
• It has thickening at the corner of the cells.
 
• The cells appear polygonal and show angular thickenings.
 
• This type of collenchyma is called collenchyma with annular thickenings.
 
• It provides more flexibility than lamellar collenchyma. 
 
• It consists of living cells and is characterized by the presence of cellulose.
 
• It is a mechanical tissue in young dicotyledonous stems and provides mechanical support and elasticity.
 
• It provides great tensile strength with flexibility to those organs in which it is found.
 
• It allows easy bending in various parts of a plant mainly young growing stem without breaking them.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Sclerenchyma:

 
 
• It is a simple permanent plant tissue.
 
• It provides mechanical stiffness and strength to the plants.
 
• It is composed of dead cells i.e non-living cells.
 
 

 
• Parenchyma: 

 
 
• These are living polygonal cells with a big central vacuole & intercellular spaces amidst them.
 
• Parenchymatous cells are responsible to create ground pith & tissue.
 
• Parenchyma contains chlorophyll and performs photosynthesis, and then it is called chlorenchyma.

• In plants, **carbon dioxide (CO₂)** enters the chloroplast through the stomata and diffuses into the stroma of the chloroplast—the site of the Calvin cycle reactions where sugar is synthesized.

• The Calvin cycle reactions can be divided into** three main stages**: carbon fixation, reduction, and regeneration of the starting molecule.
 
• The **carbohydrate products** of the Calvin cycle are the** three carbon sugar phosphate molecules** or the **triose phosphates (G3P)**. The products formed after a **single turn of the Calvin cycle** are **3 ADP, 2 glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P) molecules, and 2 NADP+.**

• **Monoecious plants** have both male (androecium) and female (gynoecium) reproductive organs in the same plant.
 
• This characteristic allows monoecious plants to self-pollinate, although cross-pollination can also occur.
 
• Examples of monoecious plants include maize, cucumbers, and squash.
 
• Monoecious plants are different from dioecious plants, which have male and female reproductive organs on separate plants.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Androecium**

 
 
• The androecium is the male reproductive part of a flower.
 
• It consists of stamens, each of which has a filament topped by an anther where pollen is produced.
 
 
 
• **Gynoecium**
 
 
• The gynoecium is the female reproductive part of a flower.
 
• It consists of one or more carpels, each containing an ovary, style, and stigma.
 
• The ovary contains ovules, which develop into seeds upon fertilization.
 
 
 
• **Dioecious**
 
 
• Dioecious plants have male and female reproductive organs on separate plants.
 
• This means that a dioecious plant is either male or female, not both.
 
• Examples of dioecious plants include holly, willow, and asparagus.
 
 
 
• **Pollination**
 
 
• Pollination is the process by which pollen is transferred from the male part of a plant to the female part, allowing fertilization to occur.
 
• Pollination can be carried out by wind, water, insects, birds, and other animals.
 
• Self-pollination occurs within the same flower or plant, while cross-pollination occurs between different plants.

__
 
• **Maize** exhibits parallel venation, which is typical of monocotyledonous plants.
 
• In parallel venation, veins run parallel to each other, which is different from reticulate venation where veins form a network.
 
• Examples of plants with parallel venation include grasses, lilies, and maize.
 
• Reticulate venation is commonly found in dicotyledonous plants like China rose and Tulsi.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Venation**

 
 
• Venation refers to the arrangement of veins in the leaf blade.
 
• It is important for the identification of plant species and helps in the distribution of nutrients and water throughout the leaf.
 
 
 
• **Reticulate Venation**
 
 
• Reticulate venation is characterized by a net-like pattern of veins.
 
• It is commonly found in dicots such as China rose, Tulsi, and Coriander.
 
• In this type of venation, the main vein (midrib) branches into secondary veins which further branch into tertiary veins forming a network.
 
 
 
• **Parallel Venation**
 
 
• Parallel venation is characterized by veins running parallel to each other.
 
• It is typical of monocots such as Maize, wheat, and other grasses.
 
• In this type of venation, veins do not form a network but run parallel from the base to the tip of the leaf.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Plants**
 
 
• **China Rose (Hibiscus rosa-sinensis)** - Exhibits reticulate venation.
 
• **Tulsi (Ocimum tenuiflorum)** - Exhibits reticulate venation.
 
• **Maize (Zea mays)** - Exhibits parallel venation.
 
• **Coriander (Coriandrum sativum)** - Exhibits reticulate venation.

questions.question: The green plants in a terrestrial ecosystem capture about ________ percent of the energy of sunlight that falls on their leaves and convert it into food energy.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is__** Option 3**__. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• When **sunlight falls **on the leaves of **green plants, a process called photosynthesis occurs**.
 
• **Photosynthesis** is the biological process by which plants convert **sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water into glucose (a form of sugar) and oxygen.** This process takes place in specialized structures within **plant cells** called **chloroplasts,** which contain a pigment called** chlorophyll that gives plants their green color.**
 
• **During photosynthesis,** **chlorophyll** absorbs the energy from **sunlight.**
 
• This energy is used to** power a series** of** chemical reactions **that convert** carbon dioxide **and **water into glucose.**
 
• **The glucose** produced is then used by the plant as a **source of energy **for various **metabolic processes, such as growth, reproduction, and maintenance of cellular functions.**
 
• However, not all the energy from sunlight can be captured and converted by plants.** Sunlight** consists of a broad spectrum of **electromagnetic radiation, including visible light.**
 
• other factors such as the angle and intensity of** sunlight, the availability of water and nutrients, and the efficiency of the plant's photosynthetic apparatus can influence the amount of energy that plants capture and convert into food energy.**
 
• On average, it is estimated that green plants in a terrestrial ecosystem are able to capture and convert approximately **1 percent **of the total energy from sunlight into food energy through photosynthesis.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements about pteridophytes are correct?

Statements:

A. They include horsetails and ferns.

B. Pteridophytes are used for medicinal purposes and as soil-binders.

C. They are very advanced type of plants on earth, which evolved very recently.

D. Evolutionarily, they are the first terrestrial plants to possess vascular tissues – xylem and phloem.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only A, B and D**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Pteridophytes** include horsetails and ferns, which are vascular plants widely distributed in terrestrial ecosystems. (Source: NCERT Biology Textbook, Class 11)
 
• Pteridophytes serve ecological and economic purposes, such as being used for medicinal applications and acting as soil-binders to prevent erosion. (Source: Current Environmental Science Research)
 
• Evolutionarily, pteridophytes are the **first terrestrial plants to possess vascular tissues** like xylem and phloem for water and nutrient transportation. (Source: NCERT Biology Textbook, Class 11)
 
• Pteridophytes are ancient plants that bridge the gap between bryophytes and gymnosperms; they are not recently evolved or highly advanced plants. (Source: Evolutionary Botany Studies)

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Vascular Tissues in Plants:**

 
 
• Xylem primarily carries water and dissolved minerals, while phloem transports organic nutrients like sugars.
 
• The presence of vascular tissues marks the evolutionary advancement of pteridophytes compared to bryophytes.
 
 
 
• **Horsetails and Ferns:**
 
 
• Horsetails belong to the genus *Equisetum* and are characterized by jointed stems and spore-based reproduction.
 
• Ferns are non-flowering vascular plants with large, divided leaves known as fronds.
 
• Both horsetails and ferns are widely used in horticulture and ecological restoration projects.
 
 
 
• **Ecological Role of Pteridophytes:**
 
 
• Pteridophytes contribute to soil stabilization, especially in areas prone to erosion.
 
• They play an important role in the carbon cycle by sequestering carbon dioxide through photosynthesis.
 
• Several species are utilized for ornamental purposes due to their aesthetic foliage.
 
 
 
• **Evolutionary Importance:**
 
 
• Pteridophytes bridge the evolutionary gap between non-vascular bryophytes and seed-bearing gymnosperms.
 
• They exhibit structural adaptations such as true roots, stems, and leaves, reflecting significant evolutionary progress.
 
• Unlike bryophytes, they reproduce via spores and do not depend on water for fertilization.

questions.question: A type of asexual reproduction in which new plants are produced from roots, stems, leaves and buds is known as ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is v**__egetative propagation__**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Vegetative propagation** - It is a type of **asexual reproduction** in which new plants are **produced from roots, stems, leaves, and buds.**
 
• Since reproduction is through the vegetative parts of the plant, it is known as **vegetative propagation**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Layering **is a means of plant propagation in which a portion of an **above-ground stem grows roots** while still attached to the **parent plant** and then detaches as an independent plant. 
 
• **Budding, or bud grafting**, is a form of vegetative or clonal plant propagation by which an **exact replica** of the parent plant is produced.
